conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and help you feel supported during these first weeks with your baby. Today I’ll be using a short, validated tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. It’s just ten gentle questions about how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days; it helps us pick up on any signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up after childbirth, and it includes a question about self-harm so we can keep you safe. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me you’re in danger, and there are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. If any question feels hard, just tell me and we can pause or re-word it. Ready to begin?

1. Over the last seven days, have you still been able to look forward to things you used to enjoy, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

[Voice a little quiet, eyes flicking to the baby carrier beside me.]

I… I mean, there are a few things that still sound nice—like when my sister offers to bring over coffee or when I get twenty minutes to flip through a magazine—but even when I do them, it’s like the color’s been turned down. I can still laugh, sort of, but it fades fast and then I feel flat again. So the enjoyment is there, just… dimmer, I guess.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[Small shrug, eyes on the floor.]

Most days I can still laugh a little—like when the baby makes those silly milk-drunk faces—but it doesn’t feel as easy or genuine as before. The laughter kind of catches in my chest and then I’m tired again.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[Hands twisting in my lap.]

Not really… I mean, I try to tell myself I should be excited about little things—like taking the baby for a walk or having my favorite show on later—but when I picture them, the spark just isn’t there. I still do them, hoping the enjoyment will show up, but mostly I feel flat, like I’m going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[Voice drops, eyes sting.]

Yeah… I do that a lot. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong,” or “I’m a terrible mom.” Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk and I sat on the kitchen floor crying because I kept telling myself I’d just ruined her whole day. Rationally I know accidents happen, but the guilt just piles on anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[Shoulders tense, rocking slightly.]

Pretty much all the time. Even when she’s sleeping soundly, I’m staring at the monitor thinking, “Is she breathing? Did I fasten the swaddle too tight?” My heart races over every little grunt or hiccup. I know most of it’s probably normal baby stuff, but I can’t shut the worry off—it just loops in my head.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[Voice quivers, arms wrapping around myself.]

Yes… it hits out of nowhere. Like last night, I was just folding her tiny onesies and suddenly I couldn’t breathe—my chest got tight, heart pounding, like something awful was about to happen. It lasted maybe ten minutes, but there was no real reason. I kept telling myself, "You're safe, she's safe," but the fear just sat on me.
Things have been getting on top of me

[Exhales shakily, rubbing my temples.]

Yes… most days feel like I’m drowning in small tasks. Feed, burp, change, soothe, pump, wash bottles, try to eat something—then it starts over. I make lists, but the list just grows while I’m still stuck on the first line. Sometimes I end up crying while I rock her because I can’t see how I’ll ever catch up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[Looking away, voice rough.]

Yeah… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps circling through everything I might be doing wrong, or I’ll jerk awake thinking I heard her cry. Even when she sleeps a four-hour stretch, I’m still staring at the ceiling most of the night. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and when I finally do, I wake up every hour or two with my heart racing.
I have felt sad or miserable

[Swallowing hard, eyes welling up.]

Most of the time. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a weight sitting on my chest. I can smile for the baby, but inside it’s just this constant gray sadness that doesn’t lift. Some afternoons I end up crying while I fold laundry or just staring out the window—nothing specific triggers it, it just feels like I’m stuck under a cloud that won’t move.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods slowly, wiping a tear that’s already slipping*

Yeah… it’s happened almost every day this week. Sometimes it’s just quiet tears while I’m nursing, other times it turns into full-on sobbing when I’m alone in the bathroom. I’ll tell myself, “You don’t need to cry over this,” but the tears just come anyway.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[Shakes head quickly, eyes widening.]

No—no, never. I feel low, but I would never want to leave her or hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she needs.

Hearing how hard these early weeks have been for you-feeling flat, constantly on edge, and overwhelmed yet still trying so hard to smile for your baby-shows remarkable strength. The persistent sadness, daily tears, and sense of drowning in routine tasks tell me your emotional load right now is heavy. Wanting to feel better so you can be the mom she needs is a powerful wish, and help is within reach.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>this pervasive anhedonia.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, intense self-blame over minor incidents (spilled milk, normal baby fussing) with tearful distress, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive worry about baby's safety despite reassurance, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart, fear) occurring out of nowhere and lasting ten minutes, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to manage tasks, and crying while caring for baby, aligning with 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty: racing thoughts, repeated awakenings, persistent insomnia despite exhaustion—consistent with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, pervasive sadness that dominates daily life, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying almost daily, with episodes ranging from quiet tears to full sobbing, indicating crying occurs most of the time.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 places you well above the ≥14 cutoff indicating probable <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. You endorsed near-maximum severity on nine of ten items: pervasive low mood, loss of interest, intense self-blame, constant worry, sudden panic, feeling overwhelmed, insomnia, sadness, and frequent crying. These align with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for a major depressive episode (≥5 symptoms, same two weeks) and co-occurring anxiety. Denial of self-harm is reassuring, yet functional impairment is significant. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med>
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment options such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or an <med>SSRI</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Schedule brief daily check-ins with a trusted adult who can monitor your mood, anxiety, and ability to care for yourself and baby
4. Plan 3-4 hour blocks of protected sleep (partner/family handles night duties) to reduce <sym>sleep deprivation</sym>
5. Use 5-minute grounding or breathing techniques when <sym>panic symptoms</sym> arise
6. Contact local <med>postpartum support groups</med> or 24/7 warmline for immediate encouragement and resource linkage
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based interview, 0–3 point descriptive responses.

Presenting symptoms endorsed:
- Persistent low mood, “constant gray sadness,” daily tearfulness  
- Marked anhedonia: activities done “hoping enjoyment will show up”  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care; catastrophic thinking over minor mishaps  
- Generalized anxiety: near-continuous worry about baby’s safety, intrusive “looping” thoughts  
- Discrete panic attacks (tight chest, pounding heart, no clear trigger)  
- Overwhelmed/drowning in routine tasks; difficulty completing feed–pump–sleep cycle  
- Initial and middle insomnia linked to ruminations and hyper-vigilance to infant sounds  
- Fatigue and sense of “heaviness” on waking

Safety screen: Denies any thoughts of self-harm or desire to die; protective factor = strong wish to parent infant.

Overall pattern: High endorsement of depressive and anxiety symptoms beginning post-delivery, functionally impairing sleep, coping, and emotional availability. Meets screening criteria for probable Major Depressive Episode with Peripartum Onset and comorbid Panic/Anxiety features; no immediate self-harm risk per patient statement.

Recommendation: Refer for immediate comprehensive psychiatric evaluation; consider standardized EPDS scoring and differential (thyroid, anemia, medication effects).
